abstract: Plants exhibit large variation in reproductive strategies, from obligately sexual to exclusively asexual. Clonal vegetative reproduction is common among plants, and despite theory assuming that trade-offs exist between sexual and clonal reproduction, empirical demonstrations of trade-offs remain elusive. Here we examined whether the strength of genotypic trade-offs in white clover (Trifolium repens) depends on spatial scale of sampling, and the environmental factors that favour sexual versus clonal reproduction. We quantified genetic variation and tested for trade-offs within and among populations from North America. Within a population, we grew up to 5 clonal replicates from each of 38 genotypes collected from a population in southern Canada. Among populations, we grew up to 5 clonal replicates from each of 46 populations, collected from a 21{o} transect from southern USA to northern Canada. All plants were randomized in a single growth chamber and grown for 12 weeks while keeping resource availability constant. From each plant, we measured investment in sexual reproduction as the number of inflorescences, and investment in clonal reproduction as the number of stolons, total stolon length and leaf area. We also extracted multiple environmental variables from each population. There was substantial genetic variation for all traits at both spatial scales, but genetic variation was always greater among populations. At the within population scale, the number of inflorescences was positively genetically correlated with the number of stolons and leaf area. Among populations, the number of inflorescences was negatively genetically correlated with both stolon length and leaf area. Colder, drier, high-latitude sites were associated with increased clonality. Our results show that the strength and direction of genotypic trade-offs differs within versus among populations, with trade-offs only being apparent at the largest scale among populations. These results provide insight into when and how trade-offs evolve between sexual and clonal plant reproductive strategies.
